question: How do light-dependent reactions provide the energy carriers used by the Calvin cycle?

actual_final_response.answer_text: The light-dependent reactions convert light energy into chemical energy stored in energy carriers, and these carriers transport that energy to the Calvin cycle [ev_008] [ev_005] [ev_007]. The light-dependent reactions use light to temporarily store energy in energy carriers [ev_005] [ev_008]. Photosystems absorb light and use electron transport chains to convert energy into the chemical energy of ATP and NADPH [ev_002]. These energy-carrying molecules travel into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle reactions take place [ev_007]. The Calvin cycle then uses the energy in ATP and NADPH to convert CO2-derived molecules into G3P [ev_010]. The energy carriers are described as "full" when they carry energy from the light-dependent reactions to the Calvin cycle, and as "empty" after the energy is released, when they return to the light-dependent reactions to obtain more energy [ev_001]. The Calvin cycle is the set of reactions that use the energy stored by the light-dependent reactions to form glucose and other carbohydrate molecules [ev_011].
actual_final_response.short_answer: Light-dependent reactions store light energy in ATP and NADPH [ev_008] [ev_002], which travel to the Calvin cycle in the stroma to power carbohydrate synthesis [ev_007] [ev_011].
